steps.title: Legal position
steps.content: Under Rule 122A, no new drug may be imported except with permission from the Licensing Authority, applied for in Form 44 with a fee of fifty thousand rupees. Rule 122D separately requires Form 44 with a fee of fifteen thousand rupees for fixed-dose combinations, with data per Appendix VI of Schedule Y. For a phytopharmaceutical drug, Appendix I-B requires identification and authentication of plant source, pharmacological data, clinical trial protocols, regulatory status abroad, and post-marketing surveillance reports every six months for two years. Category matters: a classical First-Schedule formulation follows the Ayurvedic drug regime outside Schedule Y; a purified standardised fraction with defined chemical markers typically falls under the phytopharmaceutical route of Appendix I-B.

steps.title: Protection / action route
steps.content: The concrete route is to file Form 44 with the Licensing Authority defined in Rule 21(b), accompanied by the prescribed fee and the data package corresponding to the product type. For a phytopharmaceutical drug this means Appendix I-B Parts I and II, including clinical trial protocols, samples of pure substance and finished product (50 clinical doses), and a PMS plan. For a fixed-dose combination, Appendix VI of Schedule Y data on the combination plus its individual ingredients is needed. For an Ayurvedic formulation prepared per a classical text, different licensing under the Ayurvedic drug provisions would apply, which is not detailed in this corpus.

steps.title: Classification
steps.content: This is an Indian biodiversity and IP law question about Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS), which is the system that controls how biological resources and associated traditional knowledge can be accessed and how benefits from their use are shared. It matters here because anyone dealing with Indian biological material or traditional knowledge, especially in Ayurveda, may need formal approval before using, researching, or seeking IP over such resources.

steps.title: Legal position
steps.content: Under Section 21(1) of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) must ensure fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of the use of accessed biological resources, their derivatives, innovations, practices, and associated knowledge, on mutually agreed terms. Under Section 6, persons covered under section 3(2) of the Act must obtain prior approval of the NBA before applying for any intellectual property right based on research or information on a biological resource accessed from India or on associated traditional knowledge. Rule 13 of the Biological Diversity Rules 2024 requires such persons to apply on the NBA portal in Form 1 for research or bio-survey/bio-utilisation, and in Form 2 for commercial utilisation, with a specified fee paid electronically to the National Biodiversity Fund.

steps.title: Protection / action route
steps.content: Concretely, if you are a person covered under section 3(2) of the Act and you want to access Indian biological resources or associated knowledge for research, bio-survey, bio-utilisation, or commercial use, you must first file an application on the NBA web portal in Form 1 or Form 2 (as applicable) and pay the application fee (Rs 10,000 for individuals, Rs 20,000 for entities) under the First Schedule of the Biological Diversity Rules 2024. If you also want to obtain an IP right based on that material, you need prior NBA approval under Section 6 before the IP is granted. The benefit sharing you owe will be decided by the NBA, and for commercial use of IP, the ABS Guidelines indicate monetary benefit sharing of up to one percent of annual gross ex-factory sale price, with 25 percent extra where traditional knowledge is involved, plus possible upfront payments for high-value or threatened resources.

steps.title: Classification
steps.content: This is a conceptual IP-law question, not a question about classifying any specific product. The reason it matters is that Indian law treats trademarks and Geographical Indications (GIs) as different kinds of legal rights with different rules.

steps.title: Legal position
steps.content: Under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, a GI is a sign that shows goods come from a particular territory, region or locality, where a specific quality, reputation or other characteristic is due essentially to the geographical environment, including natural and human factors (Section 11(2)(a)). By contrast, under Section 9 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a trademark is a sign that distinguishes one person's goods or services from another's. The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the GI Act explains that the law was made specifically to protect the interests of producers of geographically linked goods and to keep unauthorised persons from misusing such names (page 30).

steps.title: Protection / action route
steps.content: For a trademark, the owner applies to the Trade Marks Registry and gets the exclusive right to use the mark for their goods, which can be assigned or licensed to others. For a GI, an association of producers or a body representing them applies to the Geographical Indications Registry (Section 11(1)), and the right cannot be assigned, transmitted, licensed, pledged or mortgaged (Section 24). GI registration lasts 10 years and is renewable, and only authorised users may use the GI; infringement actions can be brought by the registered proprietor and authorised users.

classification.label: Patent or proprietary Ayurvedic medicine
classification.rationale: Ashwagandha is a classical Ayurvedic ingredient referenced in authoritative texts. A new extraction process applied to it would make it a patent/proprietary Ayurvedic medicine rather than classical_generic, and patentability of the extraction process depends on which regulatory category the resulting product falls into.

steps.title: Classification
steps.content: This is a question about patent eligibility of a process, not a regulatory classification question. Even though Ashwagandha is a classical Ayurvedic ingredient, what matters for patenting is the process itself and whether it adds something technically new beyond what is already known. The product classification already noted (patent/proprietary Ayurvedic medicine) affects drug regulation, but patentability is a separate test under the Patents Act, 1970.

steps.title: Legal position
steps.content: Under Section 3(d) of the Patents Act, 1970, the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance, or a new property or new use of a known substance, is not an invention unless there is a significant enhancement of known efficacy; salts, esters, polymorphs, isomers and derivatives of a known substance are treated as the same substance unless they differ significantly in efficacy. The evidence also states that for an invention to be patentable it must involve an inventive step, meaning a technical advance or economic significance not obvious to a person skilled in the art. Because Ashwagandha and its constituents are known, a new extraction process would need to either produce a product with significantly enhanced efficacy or represent a non-obvious technical advance to pass these tests.

steps.title: Protection / action route
steps.content: The route is to file a patent application with the Indian Patent Office under the Patents Act, 1970, ensuring the claims are directed to the process (which is a patentable category) rather than to the Ashwagandha substance itself. Section 10(5) requires that all claims relate to a single inventive concept, so the application should focus on the specific extraction steps that deliver the technical advance. Separately, if the extracted product is to be marketed, the applicant must also comply with the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 requirements for phytopharmaceutical drugs, which require detailed data on the extraction process, quality specifications, and characterisation of the final purified fraction. As a defensive measure, the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) documents India's traditional knowledge including Ayurveda to prevent misappropriation of such knowledge at international patent offices.

steps.title: Jurisdiction note
steps.content: This answer reflects the position under Indian law only, based solely on the evidence provided. International patent regimes, foreign patent offices, and cross-border ABS or biodiversity rules are outside the scope of the evidence in this corpus.

steps.title: Classification
steps.content: This question is about patent eligibility for a whole plant (Ashwagandha) under Indian law, not about classifying a product. It matters because plants as living things sit at the boundary of patent law and a separate plant variety protection law, and the route you pick decides whether you can get any rights at all.

steps.title: Legal position
steps.content: Under Section 3(j) of the Patents Act, as explained in the Manual of Patent Office Practice, plants in whole or in any part thereof, seeds, varieties and species, and essentially biological processes are not inventions and so cannot be patented. The same provision also says microorganisms (other than those merely discovered in nature) may be patentable. The law gives plant varieties a different protection regime under the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001.

steps.title: Protection / action route
steps.content: Because Section 3(j) bars patents on plants themselves, the correct route for protecting a new Ashwagandha variety is the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001, not the Patents Act. A patent application covering the plant itself would be refused as not being an invention. If your invention only uses Ashwagandha (for example an extract or a formulation) and you want patent protection for that, the patent route is open, but biodiversity and traditional knowledge compliance (Biological Diversity Rules 2024, Forms 7 and 9) may also apply before filing or commercialisation.

steps.title: Jurisdiction note
steps.content: This sets out the position under Indian law only. International regimes such as PCT, EPO practice, or UPOV are outside this corpus and have not been considered.

steps.title: Classification
steps.content: This is a patentability question for a topical Ayurvedic cosmetic/cream formulation. The open factual issue flagged above (whether the cream exactly matches a First Schedule text, or is the user's own formulation) matters because the answer changes substantially between these two scenarios - so both are addressed below.

steps.title: Legal position
steps.content: Under Section 3(p), an invention that is traditional knowledge, or an aggregation/duplication of known properties of a traditionally known component, is not patentable - neem's skin/pesticidal properties are explicitly cited as an example, and the Examiner consults TKDL. Under Section 3(d), a mere new form or new use of a known substance (which would capture a new cosmetic use of neem) is not patentable unless there is significant enhancement of efficacy. Under Section 3(e), a mere admixture of ingredients is not patentable unless it produces a synergistic effect beyond the sum of individual effects. If your cream is exactly as in a First Schedule text, it sits squarely in the Section 3(p) bar. If it is your own formulation of neem with other ingredients, you still face the Section 3(e) synergy requirement and, depending on claims, the Section 3(d) enhanced-efficacy requirement.

steps.title: Protection / action route
steps.content: To pursue a patent, you must show one of three things in the specification with comparative data: (a) synergy between the neem and other components (Section 3(e)); (b) significantly enhanced efficacy over known neem use (Section 3(d)); and/or (c) that the claimed subject-matter is not mere aggregation of a traditionally known component's properties (Section 3(p)). The Manual of Patent Office Practice requires a specific utility and synergistic/enhancement data in the description, supported by disclosure. Separately, if any biological resource (neem plant material) or traditional knowledge was accessed, the Biological Diversity Rules 2024 require disclosure of source, geographical location, prior patent filings, and traditional knowledge details before grant.

steps.title: Classification
steps.content: This is not a question about classifying a specific product. It is a definitional question about an institutional mechanism — the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) — used in India to protect traditional medicinal knowledge from being patented abroad.

steps.title: Legal position
steps.content: The evidence describes TKDL as a pioneering initiative of India created to protect Indian traditional medicinal knowledge and prevent its misappropriation at international patent offices the cited source. It is a proprietary database of the Government of India, jointly held by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, NISCAIR (CSIR), and the Department of Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy the cited source. TKDL converts existing Indian traditional knowledge from Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Yoga, and other systems — available in Hindi, Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian, and Urdu — into five international languages (English, French, German, Spanish, Japanese) so that patent examiners worldwide can search it as prior art the cited source. It contains approximately 0.226 million medicinal formulations spread across 34 million A4 pages, including Ayurvedic, Unani, Siddha, and Yoga formulations the cited source.

steps.title: Protection / action route
steps.content: TKDL functions as a defensive mechanism rather than something a user registers with. Patent examiners in India use it under Section 3(p) of the Patents Act to reject claims that amount to traditional knowledge or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components — the Manual of Patent Office Practice cites turmeric's wound-healing properties and neem's pesticidal properties as examples the cited source. Internationally, TKDL is made available to foreign patent offices through access agreements so they can locate Indian prior art and reject patent applications that misappropriate it the cited source. TKDL is also recommended as a model for replication by other countries, with WHO consultations referring to it the cited source.

steps.title: Jurisdiction note
steps.content: This answer reflects the position under Indian law and the institutional framework described in the evidence above. International patent regimes, foreign patent office procedures, and bilateral TKDL access agreements with other countries are referenced only as far as the Indian-side evidence describes them, and any matters outside this corpus are not covered.

steps.title: Classification
steps.content: This is not a question about classifying a specific product. It is a definitional question about an institutional mechanism — the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) — used in India to protect traditional medicinal knowledge from being patented abroad.

steps.title: Legal position
steps.content: The evidence describes TKDL as a pioneering initiative of India created to protect Indian traditional medicinal knowledge and prevent its misappropriation at international patent offices the cited source. It is a proprietary database of the Government of India, jointly held by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, NISCAIR (CSIR), and the Department of Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy the cited source. TKDL converts existing Indian traditional knowledge from Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Yoga, and other systems — available in Hindi, Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian, and Urdu — into five international languages (English, French, German, Spanish, Japanese) so that patent examiners worldwide can search it as prior art the cited source. It contains approximately 0.226 million medicinal formulations spread across 34 million A4 pages, including Ayurvedic, Unani, Siddha, and Yoga formulations the cited source.

steps.title: Protection / action route
steps.content: TKDL functions as a defensive mechanism rather than something a user registers with. Patent examiners in India use it under Section 3(p) of the Patents Act to reject claims that amount to traditional knowledge or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components — the Manual of Patent Office Practice cites turmeric's wound-healing properties and neem's pesticidal properties as examples the cited source. Internationally, TKDL is made available to foreign patent offices through access agreements so they can locate Indian prior art and reject patent applications that misappropriate it the cited source. TKDL is also recommended as a model for replication by other countries, with WHO consultations referring to it the cited source.
